verdict.rationale: The phrase 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) recurs across seven New Testament passages (Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:2, Luke 24:1, John 20:1, John 20:19, Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2), and in the four gospel occurrences it explicitly marks the resurrection morning, which is a dense and stable lexical pattern. Acts 20:7 attaches that same first-day phrase to a corporate gathering 'having been gathered together' (synegmenon, a completed action whose result still stands, the perfect passive form) to break bread, and Revelation 1:10 supplies the only canonical adjective 'Lord's' or 'belonging to the Lord' (kuriakos) applied to a day. However the word-forms themselves do not legislate primacy: 'Lord's' (kuriakos, G2960) is near-hapax (a word that occurs only once or nearly so in the entire Bible) with two New Testament occurrences and does not on its own specify which day; 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) uses 'week' or 'sabbath' (sabbaton, G4521) as the counting term for week without ever declaring a binding shift from the seventh day; and Colossians 2:16, Romans 14:5, and Galatians 4:10 affirmatively warn against judging by sabbaths or by reckoning days, which is the lexical hinge for a no-special-day reading. So the first-day rhythm and the resurrection-morning association are lexically dense (tightly packed in the wording), but the further claim that this is the appointed gathering day is a synthesis the words permit rather than impose.

scripture.force: The date phrase 'on the first of the week' (te mia ton sabbaton) frames a gathering 'having been gathered together' (synegmenon, the perfect passive participle, a completed action whose result still stands, of 'to gather' (synago)) whose stated purpose is 'to break bread' (klasai arton). This is the clearest lexical link between the first day and a corporate assembly, but the day is named only by its position in the week, with 'sabbath' or 'week' (sabbaton) serving as the counting term, and the verse does not legislate a reason such as honoring the resurrection or assign primacy over any other day.

'On the first of every week' (kata mian sabbatou) governs an instruction that each person ('each one' (hekastos)) set aside and store up ('storing up' (thesaurizon)) for a collection ('collection' (logeia)) 'by himself' (par heauto). The temporal marker matches the first-day phrase of Acts 20:7, yet the action described is individual home laying-aside rather than a corporate worship act, so the verse supports a first-day rhythm of the believer's life but does not by itself establish an appointed gathering on that day.

'I came to be in the Spirit on the Lord's day' (egenomen en pneumati en te kuriake hemera) supplies the only canonical use of 'Lord's' or 'belonging to the Lord' (kuriakos, G2960) applied to a day. The adjective means belonging to or pertaining to the Lord, parallel to its only other New Testament use 'the Lord's supper' (kuriakon deipnon) in 1 Corinthians 11:20. The word-form itself does not specify which calendar day, so equating 'the Lord's day' (te kuriake hemera) with the first day is an inference from canonical context, not a fact the word alone carries.

'It being evening then on that day, the first of the week' (ouses oun opsias te hemera ekeine te mia sabbaton), the disciples are together behind shut doors when the risen Christ stands among them. The same 'first of the week' (mia sabbaton) phrase recurs, and the scene places a resurrection appearance on the first day, supplying the narrative basis for associating that day with the resurrection. The text reports an event, however, and does not legislate a recurring appointed day.

'After the sabbath, at the dawning toward the first of the week' (opse de sabbaton te epiphoskouse eis mian sabbaton) places the discovery of the empty tomb on the first day. The 'first of the week' (mia sabbaton) phrase is fixed here in a resurrection setting, which is one of four gospel attestations of the same construction marking the same calendar moment.

'On the first of the week Mary Magdalene comes early' (te de mia ton sabbaton Maria he Magdalene erchetai proi) again uses the 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) phrase to mark the resurrection morning. Combined with Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:2, and Luke 24:1, the four gospels lexically converge on this exact phrase as the moment of the resurrection report.

'Therefore let no one judge you in food and drink or in respect of feast or new moon or sabbaths' (me oun tis humas krineto en brosei kai en posei e en merei heortes e neomenias e sabbaton). The dictionary form 'sabbath' or 'week' (sabbaton, G4521) appears in a list of calendar markers the Colossians are instructed not to be judged by, which is the lexical hinge for a reading in which no calendar day is binding on the believer.

'For one esteems one day above another, another esteems every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind' (hos men gar krinei hemeran par hemeran, hos de krinei pasan hemeran. hekastos en to idio noi plerophoreistho). The dictionary form 'day' (hemera, G2250) is paired with 'to judge' or 'to esteem' (krino), and the verse explicitly assigns the matter to individual conviction ('let him be fully convinced' (plerophoreistho)), which the no-special-day reading uses as a direct lexical complication to any appointed-day claim.

'You observe days and months and seasons and years' (hemeras paratereisthe kai menas kai kairous kai eniautous). The verb 'to observe scrupulously' (paratereo, G3906) carries the sense of observing scrupulously, and the catalogue of time units is given a negative cast in the surrounding rebuke. This text constrains how strong an appointed-day claim can be lexically pressed without colliding with the apostolic warning.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase 'on the first of every week' (kata mian sabbatou) marks the first day, but 'let each set aside by himself' (par heauto titheto) describes individual home storage for a 'collection' (logeia) rather than a corporate assembly. This complicates the appointed gathering claim and is addressed by observing that the verse establishes a first-day rhythm and pairs with the corporate gathering of Acts 20:7, while the gathering element itself rests on Acts, not on this verse.

'Lord's' or 'belonging to the Lord' (kuriakos, G2960) names a day belonging to the Lord but does not lexically identify which day, so the verse cannot by itself prove first-day primacy. This is addressed by treating Revelation 1:10 as neutral evidence: it attests a named Lord's day in the canon, and combining it with the 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) texts identifies the day, but the identification is canonical inference rather than lexical equation.

The counting term inside the date phrase is 'sabbath' or 'week' (sabbaton, G4521), the same dictionary word used for the seventh-day sabbath, which a seventh-day reading exploits to argue the sabbath term is never displaced. This is addressed by observing that 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) is an idiom (a fixed phrase whose meaning is not the simple sum of its words) where 'sabbaton' means week, not the sabbath day, and the action assigned to the first day here is the gathering to break bread, distinct from any seventh-day rest observance.

'Sabbath' or 'week' (sabbaton, G4521) is listed alongside feast and new moon as items by which the believer is not to be judged. The first-day reading addresses this by noting that the prohibition concerns judgmental imposition of Mosaic calendar observance, not the spontaneous emergence of a new first-day pattern; the no-special-day reading takes the same verse as ruling out any calendar day having binding status. Both readings are lexically defensible from the words themselves.

The text explicitly assigns day-esteem to individual conviction ('let him be fully convinced' (plerophoreistho), fully convinced in his own mind), which on its face complicates an appointed-day claim. It is addressed by limiting the verse to disputed-matters territory and by noting that 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) in Acts 20:7 is treated as practice rather than as judgmental imposition, but the no-special-day lens reads Romans 14:5 as the controlling principle that any binding appointed-day language overreaches the lexical data.

'To observe scrupulously' (paratereo, G3906) is used negatively for observing days, months, seasons, years. This is addressed by reading the warning as targeting return to Mosaic-calendar observance under compulsion, leaving a free first-day pattern lexically unaddressed by the verse; the no-special-day lens takes it as a general caution that any prescribed day risks the same critique. The words themselves do not adjudicate which scope is intended.

'Sabbath-rest' or 'sabbath-keeping' (sabbatismos, G4520) is a New Testament hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) that redirects sabbath imagery to an end-time, future rest entered by faith. This neither prescribes nor abolishes a weekly day, and is addressed by noting that the dictionary form reframes sabbath as participation in God's rest rather than calendar observance, which is compatible with either a first-day reading or a no-special-day reading and therefore does not settle the question.

variants.note: The orchestrator bundle reports no variant units (places where Greek manuscripts differ on the wording) bearing on the date phrase or on 'Lord's' (kuriakos), and not_in_ecm_scope is true for these New Testament passages outside 3 John (meaning the critical edition of New Testament textual variants, the ECM apparatus, does not yet cover these books). The apparatus marks (notes flagging textual variants) in the supplied text (raised dots on 'our' (hemon) in Acts 20:7, 'if' (ean) in 1 Corinthians 16:2, 'first' (mia) in John 20:19) do not touch the dictionary forms that carry the verdict, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Combines the four-gospel resurrection-morning attestation of 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) (Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:2, Luke 24:1, John 20:1) with the first-day evening gathering of John 20:19, the first-day breaking of bread in Acts 20:7, the weekly first-day giving rhythm of 1 Corinthians 16:2, and the named 'the Lord's day' (kuriake hemera) of Revelation 1:10. On this reading the lexical pattern is dense enough that the first day is the appointed Christian assembly day in honor of the resurrection, even though no single verse legislates it as such.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: no special day prescribed (Romans 14, Colossians 2 reading)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Holds that Romans 14:5 assigns day-esteem to individual conscience ('let him be fully convinced' (plerophoreistho)), Colossians 2:16 explicitly forbids letting anyone judge in respect of sabbaths, and Galatians 4:10 warns against observing days, months, seasons and years. On this reading the first-day texts attest practice and freedom, not a binding appointment, and 'the Lord's day' (kuriake hemera) of Revelation 1:10 names a day belonging to the Lord without prescribing it for the church.

Argues that 'sabbath' or 'week' (sabbaton, G4521) remains the counting term in every New Testament date phrase and is never lexically displaced by a new legislated day; that the Decalogue command (Exodus 20:8) stands; and that 1 Corinthians 16:2 concerns home storage rather than corporate worship. On this reading the first-day texts describe occasional practice rather than a binding shift of the appointed day.

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses can be derived from the same lexical data without doing violence to the words. The first-day reading is supported by the convergence of 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) with resurrection narrative and with gathering verbs, the no-special-day reading is supported by the Pauline freedom texts, and the seventh-day reading is supported by the non-displacement of 'sabbath' or 'week' (sabbaton) as a counting term. The verdict turns on synthesis rather than on any single word-form.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine how the New Testament uses the phrase 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) and the adjective 'Lord's' or 'belonging to the Lord' (kuriakos), and what day, if any, the texts associate with Christian gathering and with the resurrection.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem asserts three loaded conclusions at once: that the first day is appointed, that it is the gathering day, and that the reason is honoring the resurrection. The lexical data attests first-day gathering as practice (Acts 20:7, John 20:19), a fourfold gospel association of the first day with the resurrection morning, and a named Lord's day (Revelation 1:10), but does not lexically supply the appointed status or the stated honor-the-resurrection rationale as a binding prescription. The verdict was derived on the original stem; the neutral rephrasing is recorded only to expose the embedded assumptions.

lay_summary: The question hangs on a small set of New Testament texts that point in a consistent direction without nailing every claim shut by themselves. The Greek phrase 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) appears in all four gospels at the resurrection morning (Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:2, Luke 24:1, John 20:1), in the evening gathering of John 20:19 where the risen Jesus appears, in Acts 20:7 where believers come together to break bread, and in 1 Corinthians 16:2 where Paul tells each person to set money aside on that day. Revelation 1:10 then gives the only place where a day is named the Lord's day, using the adjective 'belonging to the Lord' (kuriakos), which simply means belonging to the Lord and does not by itself say which calendar day is meant. Two lexical facts explain why this still ends up disputed. First, the word that counts the days, 'sabbath' or 'week' (sabbaton), is the same word used for the sabbath, so a seventh-day reading argues the older day was never replaced. The reply is that 'first of the week' (mia ton sabbaton) is a fixed idiom where the word means week, not sabbath. Second, three other passages cut directly against any binding day. Colossians 2:16 says let no one judge you in respect of sabbaths, Romans 14:5 says one esteems one day above another, another esteems every day alike, let each be fully convinced in his own mind, and Galatians 4:10 rebukes those who observe days and months and seasons and years using a verb for scrupulous observance, 'to observe scrupulously' (paratereo). So three readings can stand on the words themselves: a first-day reading that treats the convergence of resurrection morning, evening gathering, weekly giving, and the named Lord's day as decisive; a no-special-day reading that treats day-esteem as a matter of conscience; and a seventh-day reading that holds the sabbath term was never displaced. The plain words support a real first-day pattern of meeting and a clear resurrection-morning association, yet the fuller claim that the first day is appointed and that its purpose is to honor the resurrection has to be assembled from several passages rather than read off any single verse. That is the lexical root cause of the dispute: a dense pattern combined with explicit freedom texts that the words themselves do not rank.
